lessons.title: The Original Six
lessons.objective: Name the six teams and understand why they shaped hockey.

payload.prompt: Match the Original Six team to its city.

pairs.definition: The only U.S. city in the Original Six; known for a blue-collar style.
Madison Square Garden team; iconic in the biggest U.S. market.
Motor City team; five Stanley Cups in this era.
Canadian powerhouse; last won the Cup in 1967.
Most dominant team of the era; 15 Cups in franchise history.
Windy City; built around a dynasty of forwards.

explanation.summary: These six teams ruled from 1942 to 1967. No other team existed in the NHL during this period.
explanation.sayThisLine: The Original Six era is when hockey was pure: six teams, no expansion, brutal competition.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The Canadiens are from Montreal, right? They've been around forever.

payload.question: How would you respond?

options.text: Yes. The Canadiens started in 1909, the oldest franchise in the NHL.
I think they're from Toronto.
They're from the Original Six but I'm not sure where.

payload.translation: Montreal Canadiens, founded 1909. The most storied franchise in hockey history.

followUps.line: How many Cups have they won?
followUps.why: The Canadiens have 24 Stanley Cups, the most in NHL history.

followUps.line: Are they still good?
followUps.why: They struggle more now but have incredible history.

payload.prompt: Match the Original Six era milestone to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The year the NHL began restricting itself to six teams; all others folded or merged.
The NHL doubled in size, ending the Original Six era and opening hockey to new cities.
A quarter-century with the same six teams; no new franchises, brutal rivalries.

explanation.summary: The Original Six lasted 1942–1967, a unique period of hockey history.
explanation.sayThisLine: When the Original Six era ended, the game exploded. New cities, new stars, new dynasties.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The Leafs haven't won the Cup since 1967. What's that about?

payload.question: What is she explaining?

options.text: The Leafs won their last Cup in 1967, the same year the Original Six era ended.
The Leafs have never won a Stanley Cup.
The Leafs only won during the Original Six era.

payload.translation: Toronto's drought spans 57+ years. Their last Cup was in 1967, when the NHL was just six teams.

followUps.line: Have they come close since then?
followUps.why: Shows her team's near-misses and heartbreak.

followUps.line: Did the league get harder after 1967?
followUps.why: Expansion diluted talent and made winning tougher for existing teams.

lessons.title: Expansion and Sun Belt Hockey
lessons.objective: Explain how the NHL grew from six teams to 32.

payload.prompt: Order the major NHL expansion waves.

items.text: 1967: Six teams double to 12. LA, SF, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Minnesota, St. Louis join.
items.why: The Original Six break up. The league doubles in size.

items.text: 1970s–1980s: Atlanta, Kansas City, Vancouver, Buffalo, Washington and others join.
items.why: Gradual growth; some teams fold or relocate.

items.text: 1991–1999: San Jose, Tampa Bay, Florida, Nashville, Atlanta again, Minnesota again, Columbus.
items.why: Hockey reaches the South and expands into Sun Belt markets.

items.text: 2017–present: Vegas, Seattle and Utah round out 32 teams.
items.why: The NHL reaches its modern state with balanced conferences and divisions.

explanation.correct: Perfect. That is the arc: one era, then explosion, then gradual fills to 32.
explanation.incorrect: The NHL grew in waves: first the 1967 double, then Sun Belt moves, then western expansion.
explanation.sayThisLine: The league started with six teams in two countries. Now 32 teams reach coast to coast.

payload.prompt: What triggered the NHL to expand from six teams in 1967?

options.text: The league wanted to compete with other sports and reach new cities for fans and profit.
Players demanded higher salaries.
Ice rinks became cheaper to build.

explanation.correct: Right. Expansion was about growth: new markets, new arenas, new revenue streams.
explanation.incorrect: The NHL expanded to compete with other sports (NBA, NFL) and tap into American cities like Los Angeles and Philadelphia.
explanation.sayThisLine: Expansion made hockey a continental sport. Before 1967, it was mostly Canadian.

payload.prompt: Match the expansion era to its main feature.

pairs.definition: The Original Six doubled overnight; six new franchises in U.S. and Canadian cities.
Teams in warm-weather southern cities (Tampa, Florida, Arizona, Vegas) to reach new fans.
Recent moves to Seattle and Utah to complete the Pacific presence.

explanation.summary: The NHL went from a regional northern league to a continental giant.
explanation.sayThisLine: Sun Belt teams in Vegas, Arizona and Tampa showed hockey could thrive anywhere.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Vegas won the Cup in only their sixth season. How is that even possible?

payload.question: What is she marveling at?

options.text: A brand-new franchise, built from scratch, won the championship faster than most teams ever do.
Vegas had unfair advantages in the expansion draft.
The Cup has become easier to win.

payload.translation: Vegas's rapid success is historic. Most franchises take decades to build a Cup team. Vegas did it in six seasons.

followUps.line: Who was their first coach?
followUps.why: Gerard Gallant was brilliant; strong leadership from day one.

followUps.line: Did they have a great goalie?
followUps.why: Marc-André Fleury was elite; elite goaltending wins Cups.

lessons.title: Legends and Eras
lessons.objective: Talk about Gretzky, Orr, Lemieux, Crosby and other all-time greats.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Gretzky had like a million records. Do you think anyone will ever touch them?

payload.question: What would you say?

options.text: Probably not. His goal and assist records are so far ahead that modern records might never break them.
Of course. Sports records are broken all the time.
I don't know anything about Gretzky.

payload.translation: Gretzky's records are historic. His goal and assist totals are so dominant that many will never be broken.

followUps.line: Which era was Gretzky in?
followUps.why: The 1980s–90s; the high-scoring era before the dead puck.

followUps.line: How many goals did he score?
followUps.why: 894 goals, a record unlikely to fall soon.

payload.prompt: Match the legend to their era.

pairs.definition: 1970s defenseman; revolutionized the position by rushing the puck. Only defenseman to win the scoring title.
1980s–90s; The Great One. Holds the record for goals and assists, seemingly for eternity.
1980s–90s; Gretzky's rival and peer. Only player to win the scoring title before, during and after a cancer comeback.
2000s–present; The Next One. Three Stanley Cups with Pittsburgh. All-around greatness.

explanation.summary: Each era had its superstar. These legends defined eras of hockey.
explanation.sayThisLine: Comparing eras is fun, but each legend played by their time's rules. Gretzky, Crosby, McDavid.

payload.prompt: What does 'the Great One' refer to?

options.text: Wayne Gretzky's nickname, earned for his record-breaking career.
A generic title given to all hockey legends.
The coach who won the most Stanley Cups.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Gretzky is The Great One. No one else has that title.
explanation.incorrect: The Great One is Gretzky's exclusive nickname. His records and dominance earned him that status.
explanation.sayThisLine: When someone says 'The Great One,' they mean Gretzky. Full stop.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: I heard Crosby was called 'The Next One' when he was drafted. Does he deserve that?

payload.question: How would you explain it?

options.text: Yes. Crosby has lived up to it with three Cups, consistent excellence and leadership.
No. No one comes close to Gretzky.
It's just a nickname and doesn't mean much.

payload.translation: Crosby earned The Next One. He's a generational player with Cups, leadership and impact.

followUps.line: Is McDavid also in that conversation?
followUps.why: Absolutely. McDavid is already considered a generational talent.

followUps.line: What made Crosby special?
followUps.why: Two-way excellence, clutch performances and three Cups with Pittsburgh.

lessons.title: Miracle on Ice and the Golden Goal
lessons.objective: Explain iconic moments that defined hockey.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The Miracle on Ice was the U.S. beating the Soviet Union in 1980. Everyone still talks about it.

payload.question: Why is that such a big deal?

options.text: The Soviets were the best team in the world, and amateurs beat them at the Olympics. It changed hockey in America.
It was just a regular Olympic game.
The U.S. had never won before.

payload.translation: The Miracle on Ice (1980) was an upset so massive that it defined hockey in the U.S. for decades.

followUps.line: Did the U.S. win the gold medal?
followUps.why: Yes, they beat Finland next and took the gold.

followUps.line: Why were the Soviets expected to win?
followUps.why: The Soviet team was professional and elite; the U.S. sent amateurs.

payload.prompt: Match the iconic hockey moment to its story.

pairs.definition: U.S. Olympic team of amateurs beat the heavily favored Soviet team. Changed hockey's place in America forever.
Sidney Crosby scored in overtime for Canada to win Olympic gold in men's hockey. Became a national symbol.
The U.S. women's team won gold in 2022; the U.S. won both men's and women's gold in 2026.

explanation.summary: Iconic moments define eras. These are the ones everyone remembers.
explanation.sayThisLine: The Miracle changed America. The Golden Goal united Canada. Iconic moments stick forever.

payload.prompt: Which player scored the Golden Goal for Canada in 2010?

options.text: Sidney Crosby
Connor McDavid
Marc-André Fleury

explanation.correct: Right. Crosby scored in OT for Canada vs. USA. It was the defining moment of his career.
explanation.incorrect: Crosby's Golden Goal in the 2010 Olympics is the defining moment of modern Canadian hockey.
explanation.sayThisLine: That goal made Crosby a Canadian icon. The Golden Goal will never be forgotten.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The 2026 Olympics were wild. Both U.S. teams won gold. I've never seen that before.

payload.question: What does that mean?

options.text: Both the men's and women's U.S. hockey teams won Olympic gold medals. A historic double.
The U.S. won more games than any other country.
It was a regular outcome.

payload.translation: The U.S. sweeping both Olympic hockey golds in 2026 is rare and iconic. It defines an era.

followUps.line: Who did the men's team beat?
followUps.why: They beat Canada in the final in OT.

followUps.line: Was the women's gold as dramatic?
followUps.why: Yes, also OT. Both were nail-biters.

lessons.title: Rivalries
lessons.objective: Explain a few classic rivalries and why they matter.

payload.prompt: Match the classic NHL rivalry to its teams.

pairs.definition: The longest and deepest rivalry in hockey. Dating back to the Original Six; Montreal-Boston hatred runs deep.
Battle of Canada. Toronto and Montreal battled in the 1960s for Cup supremacy.
Edmonton and Calgary's provincial rivalry. The two Alberta cities hate each other in hockey.
Ovechkin and Crosby era. Washington and Pittsburgh playoff battles in the 2010s were epic.

explanation.summary: Rivalries give hockey extra heat. Geographic, historical or personal beef makes games matter more.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rivalries are why fans come to the rink. Bragging rights are on the line.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Whenever the Bruins play the Canadiens, it feels different. Like it matters more.

payload.question: Why is that?

options.text: History. They've played forever and hate each other. Rivalry makes every game intense.
The teams are closer in standings.
It's all the same in the modern era.

payload.translation: Old rivalries carry weight. History and emotion make Bruins-Canadiens games epic even in regular season.

followUps.line: How far back does it go?
followUps.why: Original Six era, at least. Decades of playoff battles.

followUps.line: Are playoff matchups fiercer?
followUps.why: Yes. Playoff Bruins-Canadiens is peak intensity hockey.

payload.prompt: Match the rivalry type to its example.

pairs.definition: Two cities close together hate each other (Edmonton-Calgary, Boston-New York).
Teams with decades of playoff history and tradition of fighting (Bruins-Canadiens).
Built on star players battling each other (Ovechkin-Crosby in the 2010s).

explanation.summary: Rivalries come from geography, history or personality. All three types are part of hockey.
explanation.sayThisLine: The best rivalries mix all three: location, tradition and star power.

statement.speaker: You
statement.text: I don't get why the same team matchup is always hyped. It's just another game.

payload.question: How would you correct that?

options.text: Rivalries add history and emotion. When teams hate each other, intensity rises. Stakes feel higher.
It's just marketing.
All games are the same.

payload.translation: Rivalries matter because hockey is about emotion and history, not just skill. That's the appeal.

followUps.line: Does she have a favorite rivalry?
followUps.why: Shows you're curious about her team's history.

followUps.line: Has she been to a rivalry game?
followUps.why: Those are the loudest, most intense rink experiences.

lessons.title: Hats, Beards, Octopi and the Cup
lessons.objective: Explain rink traditions and why fans love them.

payload.prompt: Match the rink tradition to where it happens.

pairs.definition: When a player scores three goals, fans throw hats onto the ice. A celebration of an incredible performance.
A Detroit tradition: fans throw an octopus on the ice for luck in playoffs. Eight legs, eight wins to the Cup.
Superstition: players don't shave during playoffs for luck. Grown for the entire playoff run.
After a playoff series ends, players from both teams shake hands. A moment of respect.

explanation.summary: Traditions are the soul of hockey fandom. They connect generations of fans.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hockey traditions are sacred. Playoff beards, octopi, hat throws: fans live for them.

payload.prompt: What happens to the Stanley Cup after the season ends?

options.text: Each winning player gets a day with the Cup to bring home and celebrate.
It stays in the NHL offices locked in a vault.
It is melted down and remade each year.

explanation.correct: Right. Every player on the Cup team gets a day with the Cup. Some days are wild celebrations at home.
explanation.incorrect: The Cup travels all summer with each winning team's players. It has been on boats, in bars, in swimming pools.
explanation.sayThisLine: A day with the Cup is a sacred hockey memory. Players take it to their hometowns for parties.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: I saw a photo of someone's dog drinking from the Stanley Cup. Is that allowed?

payload.question: How would you explain it?

options.text: Yes. Once you win the Cup, you get a day with it and can do almost anything. Even silly things like that.
No, the Cup is sacred and can't be touched like that.
Only the captain is allowed to touch the Cup.

payload.translation: The Cup is treated with reverence but also shared with a player's loved ones. Dogs, pools and parties are all part of the tradition.

followUps.line: Has the Cup ever been damaged?
followUps.why: Yes, it's been dropped, dented and lost. It's been through a lot.

followUps.line: Where is the real Cup stored?
followUps.why: The Vault of the Hockey Hall of Fame. Teams use a replica for travel.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: What's the All-Star Game? Is it like the All-Star break in other sports?

payload.question: How would you explain it?

options.text: Yes, it's a mid-season exhibition game featuring the league's best players. Fans vote them in.
It's the playoff championship game.
It's an amateur tournament.

payload.translation: The All-Star Game is a showcase and celebration. Not serious playoff hockey, just fun and star power.

followUps.line: How do players get selected?
followUps.why: Fan voting and coach selections. Coaches also nominate players.

followUps.line: Does the All-Star Game matter?
followUps.why: Not for standings, just for fun and bragging rights.

lessons.title: Hockey Slang and Chirping
lessons.objective: Decode the slang fans use and understand the etiquette of talk.

payload.prompt: Match the hockey slang to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The puck. 'He put the biscuit in the basket' = he scored.
A stickhandling move that fakes out an opponent. 'He dangled the defenseman' = amazing footwork.
A saucer pass: a soft pass that floats over the ice. 'He sauced it to the winger.'
A shot that goes off the crossbar and in. 'He ripped it bar down' = perfect shot.

explanation.summary: Hockey slang is colorful and fun. Learning it helps you sound like a fan.
explanation.sayThisLine: When you hear slang at the rink, you'll know exactly what's being said. Bar down is always a goal.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: He dangled three guys and buried it bar down. That was nasty.

payload.question: What just happened?

options.text: A player faked out three defenders with stickhandling and scored by hitting the crossbar. Incredible play.
The player was penalized.
I'm not sure what that means.

payload.translation: That's elite slang. Dangle (stickhandle), bury (score), bar down (crossbar): all signs of an amazing goal.

followUps.line: Can you describe that play back to her?
followUps.why: Use the slang: 'That dangle was sick. Bar down is pure.'

followUps.line: Did she use slang naturally?
followUps.why: Yes, and she'll notice you know it too.

payload.prompt: Match the chirping etiquette to the right behavior.

pairs.definition: Trash talk between players on the ice. Light insults, jokes and heat. Part of the game.
After a playoff series, players shake hands and show respect despite the intensity. Unwritten rule.
Chirping is okay; personal attacks on family or hateful stuff crosses it. Players self-police.

explanation.summary: Chirping is part of hockey culture, but there is a code. Heat on ice, respect off it.
explanation.sayThisLine: Chirping is fun talk. Going after family or making it mean ruins the game. Players know the difference.

payload.title: Decoding a chirp
payload.setting: You hear two players talking trash at the rink and want to understand what just happened.

exchanges.theirMessage: Did you hear what that player just said? Seemed mean.

replies.text: That's chirping. Heat on the ice is part of hockey. As long as they shake hands after, it's okay.
replies.coachNote: You explained the unwritten rule: chirp hard, respect after.

replies.text: That's harsh. Hockey players are mean.
replies.coachNote: True, but missing the context and etiquette.

replies.text: I have no idea what's happening.
replies.theirResponse: It's part of the sport, I guess.
replies.coachNote: Being lost is okay; ask and learn.

exchanges.theirMessage: But they looked like they actually hated each other.

replies.text: That's the intensity. After the game, watch: they'll often chat or shake hands. Heat on ice is different from reality.
replies.theirResponse: Oh, I get it now. It's a role.
replies.coachNote: You captured the unwritten rule perfectly.

replies.text: Maybe they do hate each other.
replies.coachNote: Possible, but usually it's just part of the game.
Honesty is fine; ask for clarification if you need it.

payload.closingNote: Chirping is sport behavior, not personal. The respect comes after the intensity.
